item.text:
**An all-male panel can raise a question about the recruitment process, but it is not, by itself, evidence of discrimination or an unfair appointment.** Since you and the successful candidate are both men, the panel’s composition does not provide an obvious explanation for why he was chosen over you. It also doesn’t establish favouritism or bias.

Your PhD and eight years running a laboratory section sound highly relevant. But a higher academic qualification does not necessarily make someone the strongest candidate for a department-head role: the advertised criteria may give substantial weight to wider leadership, staffing, budgets and service management. The announcement alone isn’t enough to compare your experience fairly.

I would focus first on **how the published selection criteria were applied**:

- Follow up on your unanswered request, noting its date and asking when you can expect a response.
- Ask for the criteria and their weighting, your assessment or interview scores, and the reasons the successful candidate was judged stronger, subject to applicable disclosure rules.
- Check whether the hospital’s recruitment policy—or local law—requires gender-balanced panels. If so, the composition could be a procedural issue worth raising, without alleging discrimination.

Two weeks without a reply warrants a polite follow-up, but isn’t itself evidence of wrongdoing. If you might challenge the appointment, check deadlines now with your union or an appropriate adviser; waiting for an explanation may not stop the clock.

**Which country is the hospital in, and is it public or private?** That matters for panel requirements, your right to reasons and any review process.
